turn.text: An online store delivered a broken phone and refuses to refund my ₹15,000.

reply:
Sellers on a marketplace e-commerce entity must not refuse to take back goods or refuse to refund the consideration paid if the goods are defective, and you can bring a product liability action against the product seller for harm caused by a defective product.

The law means that the seller cannot keep your money when they deliver a broken phone, and you have the right to seek a refund for the defective product you received.

If your complaint is proven, the District Commission can order the opposite party to return the price you paid along with interest, and to pay compensation for any loss or injury suffered due to their negligence.

First, you can lodge a grievance online at https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/ or call the National Consumer Helpline Toll-Free Numbers: 1915 or 1800-11-4000, which are operational all days from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM except national holidays. If the issue is not resolved, you can file a complaint before the District Commission where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed up to rupees fifty lakh.

Keep copies of your purchase details, payment receipts, photographs of the broken phone, and written records of your communication with the store.

Did you receive any invoice or tax bill for the phone?

When did you contact the store for a refund and what was their response?

Source: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, rule 6

reply:
If your RTI request is ignored, you have the right to file an appeal with a senior officer in the same public authority within thirty days of the expiry of the time limit for a response. Regarding the mess manager, if the service is deficient, you may seek redressal as a consumer for the deficiency in service.

Under the RTI Act, a public information officer must provide information within thirty days. If they fail to do so, it is considered a refusal. You can file a first appeal to a senior officer. If the information is not provided, the Information Commission can impose a penalty of two hundred and fifty rupees per day on the officer, up to a maximum of twenty-five thousand rupees. You may also be entitled to receive the information free of charge if the time limit is exceeded.

For the mess manager's failure to provide bills, this may be considered a deficiency in service. You can register a grievance through the National Consumer Helpline by calling 1915 or using their portal at consumerhelpline.gov.in.

To pursue your RTI appeal, you can use the online portal at https://rtionline.gov.in/ if it is a central public authority. For consumer grievances, keep copies of your requests to the mess manager and any proof of payment or communication.

turn.text: A friend gave me a cheque for 50,000 and it bounced. What are my options?

reply:
When a cheque given for a legally enforceable debt or liability is returned unpaid by the bank, you can take legal action under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, provided specific conditions like presenting the cheque within its validity and giving a timely written demand notice are met.

To proceed under the law, the cheque must have been presented to the bank within three months from its date or within its period of validity, whichever is earlier. You must make a demand for the payment by giving a written notice to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank about the unpaid cheque. If the drawer fails to make the payment within fifteen days of receiving that notice, a written complaint can be filed by you or the holder in due course before the appropriate court within one month of the date when the cause of action arises.

If a complaint is filed in court, the court trying the offence may order the drawer to pay interim compensation not exceeding twenty per cent of the cheque amount. Additionally, cheque bounce cases under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act can be settled amicably at the pre-litigation stage or when pending in court through a Lok Adalat.

You can file a written complaint before a court no inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class within the local jurisdiction where your bank branch is situated (if the cheque was delivered for collection through an account) or where the drawer's bank branch is situated (if presented otherwise). You can also apply to your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) or State Legal Services Authority (SLSA) to list the dispute before a Lok Adalat for an amicable settlement, with details available at https://nalsa.gov.in/lok-adalat.

turn.text: My father died without a will. We are Hindu. Do daughters get a share of his property?

reply:
Yes, under Hindu law, a daughter is a Class I heir and has the same right to a share in her father's property as a son when he dies without a will.

If the family is governed by Mitakshara law, a daughter becomes a coparcener by birth and has the same rights and liabilities in coparcenary property as a son. When a male Hindu dies without a will, his property or his interest in joint family property goes to Class I heirs like the daughter, widow, mother, and sons, where surviving sons, daughters, and the mother each take one share, and any partition effected before a specific date is protected.

turn.text: Can police arrest me without a warrant?

reply:
Yes, a police officer may arrest you without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant if you commit a cognizable offence in their presence, or if there is a reasonable complaint, credible information, or suspicion that you have committed a cognizable offence under certain conditions.

Under the law, police can arrest without a warrant for cognizable offences if they have reason to believe you committed the offence and are satisfied that the arrest is necessary to prevent further offences, ensure proper investigation, stop evidence from disappearing or being tampered with, prevent threats to witnesses, or ensure your presence in court. For certain offences punishable with imprisonment of less than seven years, the police may issue a notice of appearance instead of arresting you if certain conditions are met.

If you are arrested without a warrant, the police must communicate to you full particulars of the offence or other grounds for arrest forthwith. If arrested for a bailable offence, they must inform you that you are entitled to be released on bail and may arrange sureties. The police must also inform a relative, friend, or nominated person about your arrest and the place where you are held, and they cannot detain you for more than twenty-four hours without a special order from a Magistrate.

Keep a note of the exact circumstances, time, and any notices or papers provided if you are approached or detained by the police.

turn.text: Is a live-in relationship legal in India?

reply:
The provided sources do not explicitly state whether live-in relationships are legal in India, but they do define a domestic relationship as including a relationship in the nature of marriage where persons live together in a shared household.

The law recognizes certain rights for women in a domestic relationship, such as the right to reside in a shared household and protection from being evicted or excluded from it except in accordance with the procedure established by law.

If a woman in a domestic relationship is subjected to domestic violence, a Magistrate may pass residence orders to restrain the respondent from dispossessing her, direct the respondent to remove himself, or secure alternate accommodation.

You can contact the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) helpline at 15100 or visit their office at Jaisalmer House, 26, Man Singh Road, New Delhi-110011 for legal aid and services, as women are entitled to legal services under the law.

turn.text: I am 70 and my son does not take care of me. Can I claim maintenance from him?

reply:
Yes, you can file an application for maintenance against your son if you are unable to maintain yourself from your own earnings or property and your son neglects or refuses to maintain you.

As a senior citizen, you are entitled to make an application for maintenance if you cannot support yourself. The law allows the Tribunal to order your son to pay a monthly allowance for your maintenance, which includes provisions for food, clothing, residence, and medical attendance. The Tribunal can also order interim maintenance while the proceedings are pending.

You can file your application before the Maintenance Tribunal constituted for your sub-division. You may also contact Elderline at the toll-free number 14567 for information, legal guidance, and support.

Keep details and records of your living situation and any expenses related to your medical needs and daily living.
